clue.text: Battleship RAF woman redesigned

indicators.note: something redesigned has been reworked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as written

explanation.surface: A servicewoman in the Royal Air Force has been given a new look, though she ends up as a warship.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-of-war is an old term for an armed naval vessel, a fighting ship of the sailing era.

clue.text: Another touring quite empty Indian city

indicators.note: touring means going around, so the first word goes round the next piece
empty means hollowed out, so only the outside letters of the word remain

blocks.note: more means another, as in 'have some more'
'Quite!' is an exclamation of agreement meaning yes; only its outer letters are kept

explanation.surface: Another trip around an Indian city that is nearly deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite!' said in agreement means yes, a sense the solver may miss because it reads as an adverb of degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Mysore, now Mysuru, is a historic city in the southern Indian state of Karnataka.

clue.text: Sister outside a church in shade

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the sister word wraps round the next letter

blocks.note: a nun is a religious sister
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A nun stands outside a church in the shadows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shade' looks like shadow, but it is a subtle gradation of meaning. CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuance is a subtle difference or shade of meaning, as in 'shades of opinion'.

clue.text: Passing remark?

blocks.note: surface reading: a casual comment made in passing
setter's reading: passing means dying, so the remark is what someone says just before death

explanation.walkthrough: Passing is a euphemism for dying; the phrase is also used ironically for a confident claim soon proved wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a person's final utterance before dying, which is a remark made at one's passing.

clue.text: Eater - pips taken out to make starter

indicators.note: taken out suggests being pulled apart and reassembled, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner removes the seeds from fruit to serve as a first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken out' looks like removal of the pips, but nothing is removed: every letter of the two words is used.
explanation.definitionFit: An appetiser is the small first course of a meal, which is what a starter is.

clue.text: Unique description of switch saving energy

indicators.note: saving something means keeping it safe inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a switch is labelled on and off
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone describes a special switch that conserves power.
explanation.walkthrough: The switch's two settings stand side by side, and the energy symbol slips in at the point where they meet.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-off is something made or happening only once, so it is a synonym for singular or unrepeated.

clue.text: Throwing event is not ideal for a ballerina

indicators.note: throwing things scatters them, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as written

explanation.surface: An athletics throwing event is unsuitable for a ballet dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throwing event' reads as the discus or javelin, but 'Throwing' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Ninette de Valois was an Irish-born dancer who founded the Royal Ballet, so she is an example of a ballerina.

clue.text: Notice your bait working?

indicators.note: something working is in motion and being changed, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as written

explanation.surface: An angler is asked whether they have noticed the bait doing its job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: a published announcement.
explanation.definitionFit: An obituary is a newspaper notice of a death, usually with a short biography.

clue.text: Strong wind getting up breaks safety device in body of aircraft

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up means rising, so the word is read from bottom to top
breaks means bursts into, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a gale is a strong wind
a fuse protects an electric circuit

explanation.surface: A rising gale damages a safety mechanism inside a plane's structure.
explanation.definitionFit: The fuselage is the main central structure of an aeroplane, which holds crew, passengers and cargo.

clue.text: Finish second and first

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
top means first or best

explanation.surface: A race where someone finishes in both second and first place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' and 'first' look like race positions, but one is an abbreviation and the other a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop is to cease or bring to an end, a synonym for finish as a verb.

clue.text: Liven up after Sunday Mass

indicators.note: after places the liven-up word behind the day letter, so it comes second in the answer

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for Sunday
to warm up a crowd is to liven it; warm alone serves here

explanation.surface: A suggestion to brighten up the congregation once the Sunday service is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' looks like the church service, but it is the definition as a noun: a large crowd. 'after' puts the liven-up word behind the Sunday letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A swarm is a large moving crowd of people or insects, so it is a synonym for a mass.

clue.text: A deejay might assume a haughty manner

blocks.note: first meaning, cryptic: a radio deejay puts records on air, playing tunes or airs
second meaning: the idiom for behaving in a superior, snooty way

explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads the phrase literally: airs are tunes, and a disc jockey puts them on. The second is the everyday idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: To put on airs is an idiom for acting grander than one is, which matches assuming a haughty manner.

clue.text: Tell a story about Dracula, say

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
Dracula is a count, a nobleman; 'say' marks him as an example

explanation.surface: Someone is telling a tale concerning the famous vampire.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount is to narrate or relate events in detail, so it fits telling a story as a verb.

clue.text: Dog mine? Nonsense

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine
bull is slang for nonsense or rubbish talk

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the claim that a dog belongs to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mine' looks like the possessive, but it is the noun: a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit bull is a muscular terrier breed, so it is an example of a dog.

clue.text: Sloganeers, upset about circular letter, fly off the handle

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first word wraps the following letter
upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the round letter O

explanation.surface: Advertising copywriters, angered by a round-robin memo, lose their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circular letter' sounds like a mass mailing but is just the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's rag is British slang for losing one's temper, the same idiom as flying off the handle.

clue.text: One could look after the children if their parents are late

definitions.text: One could look after the children if their parents are late

blocks.note: surface reading: a childminder covering for parents who are delayed
setter's reading: late means dead, so this is an institution caring for parentless children

explanation.walkthrough: 'late' suggests unpunctual parents, but it is the sense used of someone who has died.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a home for children whose parents have died, so it looks after them in place of the parents.

clue.text: Form of neuralgia may cause spasmodic twitching in Isaac, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things going wrong, so the letters are put out of order

blocks.note: a tic is a spasmodic twitch of a muscle
taken as written

explanation.surface: Poor Isaac's twitching may be a symptom of nerve pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' joins the twitch word to Isaac, and the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sciatica is pain along the sciatic nerve in the back and leg, a kind of nerve pain.

clue.text: Knife fight about it upset Labour's leader

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word is read from bottom to top
the leader of a word is its first letter
about means going round, so the fight word encloses the other pieces

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of Labour
a set-to is a fight or argument

explanation.surface: A knife fight breaks out over a political upset for the Labour leader.
explanation.walkthrough: A set-to, British for a scrap or quarrel, opens after its first letter to take the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiletto is a short dagger with a narrow blade, so it is a type of knife.

clue.text: Pasta Hector prepared, a disaster

indicators.note: food that is prepared has been worked over and changed, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as written

explanation.surface: A man named Hector cooked some pasta and it went horribly wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A catastrophe is a sudden great calamity, a straightforward synonym for a disaster.

clue.text: From what is heard, Garden City is favourably placed

definitions.note: the answer is the adjectival phrase; 'is' belongs with the verb 'to be' around it

indicators.note: what is heard is the spoken form, so the answer matches a name said out loud

blocks.note: Welwyn Garden City is a planned town in Hertfordshire, north of London

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that a certain garden city is well situated.
explanation.walkthrough: Welwyn Garden City is an English new town in Hertfordshire; the first word of its name is pronounced like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be well in is British slang for being in a good position, especially in favour with someone.

clue.text: Drive mostly right, then left

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: proper means right or correct
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Directions for driving: largely keep right, then turn left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' and 'right, then left' read as road directions, but drive is the definition as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To propel is to push or drive something forward, a synonym of drive as a verb.

clue.text: Acknowledged everyone had debts

blocks.note: all means everyone
debts are sums owed

explanation.surface: It was admitted that every person was in debt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'debts' is a noun, but the piece wanted is the past participle: what is owed.
explanation.definitionFit: Allowed can mean admitted or conceded, as in 'he allowed that she was right', so it matches acknowledged.

clue.text: This herb may make daughter poorly

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
poorly means unwell

explanation.surface: A warning that a certain herb could make your daughter sick.
explanation.definitionFit: Dill is a feathery aromatic plant used to flavour fish and pickles, an example of a herb.

clue.text: A peculiar team game, recalled layman

indicators.note: peculiar means odd or strange, so the following word is set into an odd order
recalled means called back, so the letters are taken in the backward direction

blocks.note: taken as written
the four letters of team rearranged
RU is rugby union, the usual crossword game

explanation.surface: An odd team game is brought back, played by non-professionals.
explanation.walkthrough: RU stands for rugby union, a common crossword game.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur is a non-professional, just as a layman lacks specialist or professional training.

clue.text: Pointer, a liability? To some extent, among other things

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only part of the preceding words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across pointer, a and liability

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a pointer is somewhat of a liability.
explanation.definitionFit: Inter alia is Latin for 'among other things', used in formal writing; the definition is its literal translation.

clue.text: King in game put back in deck

indicators.note: in places the monarch letter within the game word
put back means returned the other way, so the result is read backwards

blocks.note: polo is a game played on horseback
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A royal player was put back in the line-up for a game.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into POLO after its third letter to make POLRO, which is then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The orlop is the lowest deck of a sailing ship, so it is a specific kind of deck.

clue.text: Wake in a river, river passing through York

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river
the Ouse is the river that flows through the city of York

explanation.surface: Someone describes the wash left by a boat on the river through York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wake' looks like a boat's trail on water, but it is the verb. The Ouse is the river flowing through York in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: To arouse someone is to rouse them from sleep, so it is a synonym of wake as a verb.

clue.text: Offensive individual

blocks.note: first meaning: of a remark, rudely aimed at someone
second meaning: belonging to one particular person

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a description of a rude person, but the two words are separate senses of one adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Personal remarks are insulting ones, and personal also means private or one's own, so both adjectives fit.
